metadata.narrative: create a simple agentic ai for personal mental-wellness support. id like to have - two agents: one would be a 'Mood Agent' that reads your check-ins (text or voice) to see what your emotions are. then theres an 'Intervention Agent' that suggests quick exercises, like breathing or journaling prompts - the workflow should be: the mood bot flags a really low or high mood, and then pings the intervention bot to help out - maybe I can use an NLU tool like dialogflow? and we MUST encrypt all the data and let people delete their history - if it gets confused it should ask follow up questions and if it sees someone is repeatedly low (eg 3 times in a row) it needs to escalate to a human counselor how do I test it? we could measure engagement and self-reported mood improvement. maybe just pilot it with 20 users for 2 weeks?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: A practical build for this two-agent personal mental-wellness assistant should start from the general insight behind multi-agent AI: specialized agents handling separate subtasks tend to outperform one monolithic agent trying to do everything at once.

Popular frameworks such as AutoGen, ChatDev, and LangGraph demonstrate this specialization pattern in production systems and are reasonable starting points for orchestrating your Mood Agent and Intervention Agent.

For the handoff between the two agents, there are two established design patterns: a routing-based system, where an orchestrator decides which agent to invoke based on the incoming message, and a broadcast-based system, where the message goes to all agents and each decides whether to act.

Routing is simpler to debug but creates a single point of failure if it misclassifies a message, while broadcast avoids that bottleneck at the cost of redundant processing, so a lightweight routing layer that forwards a "mood flag" event to the Intervention Agent is a reasonable choice for a two-agent pipeline.

For the Mood Agent's NLU, Dialogflow is workable because it is built around intents, entities, and contexts, and it offers built-in sentiment analysis via Google's Natural Language API that returns a positive, negative, or neutral score alongside detected intent.

Google's own documentation for this feature explicitly recommends handing off users with very negative sentiment scores to live human agents, which matches the mood-flag-to-intervention pipeline you described.

Kore.ai offers a comparable pattern, scoring utterances across six core emotions such as sadness and fear, storing them as session context, and letting developers write conditional-transition rules that trigger escalation to a live agent.

For voice check-ins, voice-based mood detection is promising but imperfect: a system analyzing combined text and audio (Cogito) reached about 77% accuracy detecting depression from intonation, energy, and pauses, and its creators describe such tools as screening aids for clinicians rather than replacements.

A privacy-conscious option is the Xpression app, which listens for acoustic features like pitch and loudness rather than recording actual words, letting it flag emotional state without storing raw speech content.

When the Mood Agent is uncertain, standard chatbot design uses a confidence-score threshold: if the intent-matching score falls below the threshold, the system triggers a fallback that asks the user to repeat or clarify, or transfers to a human.

Related design vocabulary includes "explicit confirmation" (asking the user to clarify), "implicit confirmation" (repeating details back so the user can correct a misunderstanding), and "handoff" (breaking out of the bot flow to a human agent), all of which map onto your "ask follow-up questions when confused" requirement.

No document in the evidence gathered specifies an exact "three low check-ins in a row" escalation threshold, so that particular number should be treated as a design choice to validate empirically rather than an industry standard.

The underlying escalation logic is still well precedented: Catholic Charities' "Sister Hope" chatbot stays conversational for minor concerns but automatically connects a user to a human counselor by phone once language suggests a crisis, and in its rollout 19 of roughly 2,700 participants were routed to crisis help this way.

The Appa Health pilot shows a complementary model, pairing a scripted CBT app with trained near-peer mentors supervised by licensed clinicians who serve as a bridge to professional care when a participant's risk profile changes.

For the Intervention Agent's content, deep breathing techniques such as 4-7-8 and box breathing have study support as non-pharmacological treatments for anxiety, depression, and stress, working by counteracting the fast, shallow breathing the body produces under stress.
Therapeutic journaling also has direct supporting evidence: in one 12-week online journaling program, participants reported fewer depressive symptoms and less anxiety after just one month.

Woebot is a close real-world analog to your whole concept, using CBT-style daily check-ins to track mood and deliver mood-appropriate tools, and a Stanford peer-reviewed study found significant reductions in anxiety and depression versus a control group, with 85% of participants engaging daily or near-daily.

On encryption and deletion, best-practice guidance for mental-health apps calls for encrypting data in transit and at rest, using salted/hashed authentication with multi-factor authentication, complying with HIPAA or GDPR as applicable, minimizing collected data, and maintaining a breach-response plan.

The deletion mechanics differ by storage model: on-device data is erased by deleting the app, but server-stored data requires a clearly described way for users to request removal, and EU-facing servers must meet EU data-residency rules.
For testing, two small pilots map closely onto your 20-user, two-week plan.

The Appa Health pilot enrolled just 14 adolescents over 12 weeks using the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 self-report scales plus qualitative interviews, and reported 100% of participants feeling better with over 85% willing to recommend the program.
The larger Project Cheria pilot (124 adults, 3 months) combined PHQ-9 and mood scores with objective engagement data, averaging 7.5 hours per week of use.

Following that template, a 20-user, two-week pilot should collect a validated self-report measure such as PHQ-9 at baseline and endpoint, log engagement metrics like check-in frequency and exercise completion rate, and track how many mood flags and escalations occurred, since false-escalation rates matter as much as sensitivity in a tool like this.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

A practical build for this two-agent personal mental-wellness assistant should start from the general insight behind multi-agent AI: a single monolithic agent handling both mood-reading and intervention-suggesting tends to perform worse than two specialized agents, because focused subtasks let each agent do a better job than one agent trying to do everything at once.

Popular multi-agent frameworks such as AutoGen, ChatDev, and LangGraph demonstrate this specialization pattern in production systems and are reasonable starting points for orchestrating your Mood Agent and Intervention Agent.

For the handoff between the two agents, there are two established design patterns: a routing-based system, where an orchestrator layer decides which agent to invoke based on the incoming message, and a broadcast-based system, where the message goes to all agents simultaneously and each decides whether to act.

Routing is simpler to reason about but creates a single point of failure if the router misclassifies a message, while broadcast avoids that bottleneck at the cost of more redundant processing, so for a two-agent mood-and-intervention pipeline a lightweight routing layer that forwards a "mood flag" event to the Intervention Agent is a reasonable, easy-to-debug choice.

For the Mood Agent's natural-language understanding, Dialogflow is a workable choice because it is built as an NLU engine around intents (what the user wants), entities (specifics of what they want), and contexts (how prior turns change meaning), and it also offers built-in sentiment analysis through Google's Natural Language API that returns a positive, negative, or neutral score with every detected intent.

Google's own documentation for this feature explicitly recommends handing off users with very negative sentiment scores to live human agents, which is precisely the mood-flag-to-intervention (and eventually to-counselor) pipeline you described.

Kore.ai offers a comparable pattern: its engine scores utterances on a continuous scale across six core emotions such as sadness and fear, stores these as session-level context variables, and lets developers write conditional-transition rules that steer the conversation or trigger escalation to a live agent, which is a useful alternative if Dialogflow's sentiment granularity proves too coarse.

For voice check-ins, note that voice-based mood detection is an active but imperfect technology: one MIT-derived system (Cogito) analyzing combined text and audio reached about 77% accuracy in classifying depression from intonation, energy, and pauses, and its own creators describe such tools as screening aids for clinicians rather than replacements for them.

A privacy-conscious voice option worth studying is the Xpression app, which listens for acoustic features like pitch and loudness rather than recording actual words, meaning it can flag emotional state (calm, happy, sad, angry, anxious) without storing raw speech content, a pattern your Mood Agent could adopt to minimize sensitive audio retention.

When the Mood Agent or NLU layer is uncertain, standard chatbot design uses a confidence-score threshold: if the matching score for user intent falls below the threshold, the system triggers a fallback that either asks the user to repeat or clarify, or transfers the conversation to a human, which maps directly onto your "ask follow-up questions when confused" requirement.

Related conversational-design vocabulary is useful here too: "explicit confirmation" (the assistant asks the user to clarify how to help), "implicit confirmation" (repeating details back so the user can correct a misunderstanding), and "handoff" (breaking out of the bot flow to a human agent) are all established mechanisms your fallback logic can reuse.

For escalation after repeated low mood, no single document in the evidence gathered specifies an exact "three times in a row" threshold, so this specific numeric rule should be treated as a design choice you set and validate empirically rather than an industry-standard figure, but the underlying escalation logic is well precedented.

Catholic Charities' "Sister Hope" chatbot shows a working real-world escalation pattern: it stays conversational for minor concerns but automatically connects a user to a human counselor by phone the moment language suggesting a crisis (such as mentions of death or suicide) appears, and in its rollout, 19 of roughly 2,700 participants were routed to crisis help this way.

The Appa Health pilot shows a complementary model, pairing a scripted CBT app with trained near-peer mentors who are supervised by licensed clinicians and who serve as a bridge to professional care when a participant's risk profile changes, which is a good template for what your "human counselor" step should actually connect to.

For the Intervention Agent's content, deep breathing techniques such as 4-7-8 and box breathing have psychological-study support as non-pharmacological treatments for anxiety, depression, and stress, working by counteracting the fast, shallow breathing the body produces under stress.

Therapeutic journaling also has direct supporting evidence: in one 12-week online journaling program, participants reported fewer depressive symptoms and less anxiety after just one month, with resilience gains continuing through the program, which supports using structured journaling prompts as a quick, evidence-grounded exercise.

Woebot is a close real-world analog to your whole concept, using CBT-style daily check-in conversations to track mood and deliver mood-appropriate tools, and a Stanford peer-reviewed study of it found significant reductions in anxiety and depression versus an information-only control group, with 85% of participants engaging daily or near-daily.

On encryption and deletion, best-practice guidance for mental-health apps calls for encrypting data both in transit (via TLS/SSL) and at rest, using salted/hashed authentication with multi-factor authentication, complying with HIPAA or GDPR as applicable, minimizing collected data, offering de-identification or pseudonymous use, and maintaining a breach-response plan.

On the deletion requirement specifically, the mechanics differ by storage model: if mood-check-in data lives only on-device, deleting the app deletes the data, but if it is stored on servers you must give users a clear, described way to contact you and have their data removed, and if the app is EU-facing the servers (or an equivalent legal safeguard) need to meet EU data-residency rules.

For testing, two small pilot precedents map closely onto your 20-user, two-week plan: the Appa Health pilot enrolled just 14 adolescents over 12 weeks using the PHQ-8 and GAD-7 self-report scales plus qualitative interviews, and reported 100% of participants feeling better with over 85% willing to recommend the program, while the larger Project Cheria pilot (124 adults, 3 months) combined PHQ-9 and mood scores with objective engagement data (7.5 hours/week average use) correlated against wearable physiological signals.

Following that template, a practical 20-user, two-week pilot for your app would collect a validated self-report measure (PHQ-9 or PHQ-8, optionally paired with a simple daily 1-5 mood scale) at baseline and at the two-week endpoint, log engagement metrics such as check-in frequency, completion rate of suggested exercises, and time-in-app, and track how many mood flags were raised and how many escalations were correctly or incorrectly triggered, since false escalation rates matter as much as sensitivity does in a mental-health tool of this kind.
